newsitem.title: USA: Integon down after disappointing fourth quarter.
newsitem.headline: Integon down after disappointing fourth quarter.

text.p: Shares of Integon Corp fell about 15 percent in morning trading after the company late Wednesday reported a surprising fourth quarter loss.
Integon reported a fourth quarter loss of $1.14 a share compared to Wall Street's First Call consensus estimate of a $0.39 a share profit.
Alex. Brown and Legg Mason Wood Walker downgraded the stock following the earnings news.
Shares of Integon, which specializes in non-standard, or high-risk, automobile insurance, fell 2-5/8 or about 15 percent, to 14-7/8 after a delayed opening.

Integon's results came just one day after Progressive Corp, the second-largest writer of non-standard automobile insurance in the United States behind Allstate Corp, reported better-than-expected earnings.
Progressive reported fourth quarter operating earnings of $1.18 a share compared to the First Call consensus estimate of $1.04 a share.
However, Progressive warned that it expects profit margins to decrease in 1997 as it moves to add new customers faster.
Allstate is scheduled to report fourth quarter earnings next week.
The First Call consensus estimate for Allstate is $1.10 a share compared to $0.85 a year ago.
Progressive and Allstate posted strong results in their personal auto businesses in the first nine months of 1996, helped by improving claim trends, analysts said.
"Claim trends continued to be extremely good in 1996," Conning & Co analyst Gary Ransom said.
Indeed Travelers/Aetna Property Casualty Corp earlier this week said it experienced favorable prior year loss development, primarily in the automobile bodily injury line.

"We are extremely disappointed with 1996 and especially the fourth quarter results, Integon chief executive John Head said. "However, we took, are taking, and will take actions that should result in improved performance," he said in a statement.

Head said the company has started to take more aggressive rate increases and by the end of March 1997 will have taken rate increases in states representing more than 95 percent of the company's nonstandard auto premium volume.
Other actions that have been taken include increasing minimum down payments and implementing underwriting restrictions.
"We expect these actions to have the impact of both slowing premium growth and improving profitability," he said.
"Our focus in 1997 will be on earnings, not growth," he said.
"Over the long term, Integon's goal is to grow faster than the nonstandard auto industry and report a combined ratio of below 96 percent," Head said.
The combined ratio indicates whether a company is earning a profit on the business it writes. An underwriting profit occurs when the ratio is below 100 percent.
Legg Mason analyst Diana Wehrly said Integon apparently failed to recognize that its pricing was inadequate to cover rising claims costs.
"I think what happened was there was a disconnect between the claims department and the pricing in the marketing department," she said.
